I think you misunderstand what "peer reviewed" means. In most cases, "peer review" doesn't refer directly to the invention, just the description of that invention. Imagine that I come up with a new cancer drug. I would prepare a formal writeup of my results and submit them to a journal. The journal solicits the opinions of other members of the field, who judge my paper on whether it meets certain standards - for example, whether the conclusions I make are justified by the data I've shown, if there are any alternative explanations for my results, if I've made any bad assumptions in my reasoning, if the data was analyzed properly, if there are any obvious issues of fraud, etc. They do not judge the drug itself. And they don't replicate my experiments. That all happens after peer review, and this can be done by anyone who's interested. Peer review just establishes a minimum threshold for the quality of a scientific publication - it doesn't establish that the claims in the publication are true, just that they've passed the first test of not being obviously and irredeemably flawed.

Just because something is peer reviewed, doesn't mean it's true. At the same time, if something doesn't pass peer review, it doesn't mean the claims are false.
